candidate.answerReason: Among the 90 two-digit integers, 10 have tens digit 7 and 9 have units digit 7. Removing the duplicated 77 gives 18 favorable outcomes, so the probability is 18/90 = 1/5.

methods.label: Method 1: Count the overlap once
methods.explanation:
There are \(99-10+1=90\) possible integers, all equally likely. A number containing a \(7\) must have either its tens digit or its units digit equal to \(7\).

There are \(10\) numbers from \(70\) through \(79\), and \(9\) numbers in the list \(17,27,\ldots,97\). Together these lists include every favorable number. Their only overlap is \(77\), which was counted twice, so the number of favorable outcomes is
\[
10+9-1=18.
\]
Thus the probability is \(\frac{18}{90}=\frac15\), choice B.
methods.levelReason: This uses elementary digit counting, removal of one duplicated outcome, and favorable outcomes divided by total outcomes.

methods.label: Method 2: Count numbers with no 7
methods.explanation:
It is also possible to count the opposite condition: neither digit is \(7\). The tens digit can be any of \(1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9\), giving \(8\) choices. For each one, the units digit can be any digit except \(7\), giving \(9\) choices.

Each pair of chosen digits produces exactly one two-digit integer, so there are \(8\cdot9=72\) numbers with no \(7\). There are \(90\) integers from \(10\) through \(99\), so the other \(90-72=18\) contain at least one \(7\). Therefore the probability is
\[
\frac{90-72}{90}=\frac15,
\]
choice B.
methods.levelReason: Counting the complement requires only pairing digit choices and subtracting from the total.

candidate.annotationRationale: The shared target is calculating a finite equally likely probability. Both methods use tens and ones and interpret and reduce a fraction. Overlap counting belongs only to the first method; complement counting and pairing digit choices belong only to the second.

review.mathematicalCheck: There are 90 equally likely integers. Direct counting gives 10 + 9 - 1 = 18 favorable integers, removing the duplicated 77. Independently, the complement contains 8·9 = 72 integers, again giving probability 18/90 = 1/5, choice B.
review.levelCheck: Both methods use accessible digit counting and explain completeness and multiplicity.
review.methodDistinctness: Counting an overlapping union and counting its complement provide distinct, useful approaches.
review.annotationCheck: Probability is the shared target. Place value and fractions support both methods; overlap, complement, and pairing concepts are appropriately method-local.
